title: Regression trees: predicting numbers with leaves
intro: The same tree idea, but every leaf now predicts a number: the mean of the training values in that leaf. The result is a step function you can drag yourself.
keyPoints: Same tree, different leaf: a classification leaf predicts the majority class, a regression leaf the mean \( c_m \) of the targets in that leaf.
A split minimises the weighted MSE of the children — the regression counterpart of Gini/entropy.
The prediction is a step function: constant per leaf, jumping at the split points — never a slope.
Deeper tree = finer steps = more detail but also more noise; and outside the training range a tree cannot extrapolate.

blocks.html: The questions are the same (“area below 60 m²?”), but the leaves predict a number: the mean of the target values in that leaf.

That is the best constant prediction for a group in the least-squares sense: whoever minimizes MSE over a fixed group can do no better than the mean. So the tree only searches for where the boundaries lie.

sections.title: Splitting on MSE: the leaf is always the mean

blocks.html: Two formulas: one for what a leaf predicts (the mean) and one for what a split costs (the weighted average MSE of the children):

blocks.label: leaf prediction
blocks.caption: Every leaf m predicts the mean of the n_m target values in it — the constant with the lowest MSE.

blocks.label: split cost
blocks.caption: The weighted MSE of the two children after splitting on feature j at threshold t. The tree picks the (j, t) with the lowest cost.

blocks.html: Twelve apartments, one split at area ≤ 60: left mean 181.25 (MSE 46.7), right mean 289 (MSE 1995 — still a mess). Cost: \( \tfrac{4}{12} \cdot 46.7 + \tfrac{8}{12} \cdot 1995 \approx 1346 \).
Split the right side again at area ≤ 90: leaf means 259 and 344, tree cost drops to \( \approx 37.2 \) — 36× better. Trees keep biting recursively until the brakes kick in.
Compare with gradient descent: linear models approach their optimum in small steps; a tree searches its structure with greedy splits. The brake at the end plays the same bias-variance role in both.

The cyan staircase is the tree prediction with two split points and three leaf means. Drag the sliders to the example values — \( t_1 = 60 \), \( t_2 = 90 \), \( m_1 = 181 \), \( m_2 = 259 \), \( m_3 = 344 \) — and watch the MSE chip light up green:

blocks.title: Tree with two splits: fit the staircase yourself
blocks.subtitle: Put the split points on the jumps in the data and the leaf means on the levels — the MSE drops live and lights up green at the best fit (37.2).

metrics.label: MSE (k€)²
metrics.expr: pts.reduce((s,p)=>s+((p.x < t1 ? m1 : (p.x < t2 ? m2 : m3))-p.y)**2,0)/pts.length

blocks.html: The heart of regression trees: the prediction is constant per leaf — a series of plateaus, not a slope. For data that thinks in thresholds (housing types, tax brackets) that fits better than a straight line.

Put \( t_1 \) and \( t_2 \) close together: the MSE on these twelve points can even drop (an outlier in its own leaf) while predictions on new data become arbitrary — exactly why min_samples_leaf exists.

sections.title: Depth, smoothness and the edge of the world

blocks.html: More depth = more steps: max_depth=1 is too coarse (high bias), unlimited gives every apartment its own plateau (high variance). max_depth and min_samples_leaf set your position on the bias-variance axis.

Hard ceiling: no extrapolation. The tree only knows leaf means from the training data — ask for a price at 200 m² and you get the highest known leaf mean. Sometimes a flaw, sometimes a virtue: it invents nothing.
Rules of thumb: smooth relation → linear regression usually more accurate; data that jumps in thresholds → the tree wins. And never predict far outside the training range with a regression tree.
The same API as always — only the model is now called DecisionTreeRegressor. The example trains on the twelve apartments, compares three depths and checks extrapolation:

blocks.caption: regression tree on the apartment data
blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

X = np.array([[36],[42],[48],[55],[63],[70],[78],[85],
               [93],[100],[107],[114]])   # floor area (m2)
y = np.array([178,190,172,185,255,268,252,261,
              345,338,352,341])          # price (kEUR)

for depth in (1, 2, None):
    tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=depth,
                                 random_state=0).fit(X, y)
    print('max_depth =', str(depth), '→ R2 train:',
          round(tree.score(X, y), 3),
          '| leaves:', tree.get_n_leaves())

tree2 = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=2,
                              random_state=0).fit(X, y)
for m2 in (50, 75, 100):
    print(m2, 'm2 →', tree2.predict([[m2]])[0], 'kEUR')

# extrapolation: outside the training range the tree
# simply repeats its highest leaf mean
print('200 m2 →', tree2.predict([[200]])[0], 'kEUR (no trend!)')

blocks.html: Note: max_depth=2 already scores nearly as well as the unrestricted tree, and the prediction for 200 m² is identical to that for 114 m² — the tree cannot go beyond its highest leaf.

Per split scikit-learn scans all (feature, threshold) pairs: \( O(d \cdot n \log n) \) per node — noticeably faster than an SVM kernel. Plus scale-independence: trees are the natural first candidate for tabular data.
